text: Seven minutes early out of Stevenage, according to the stop clock. Watching my bus disappear while I was still arriving on time was a lovely start to Monday.
For once I reached a seat before the driver pulled away from Hatfield. My knees appreciated the patience, even if the engine sounded rather tired.
Seats looked freshly cleaned on the St Albans bus, but the pole beside mine was sticky enough to collect fingerprints. Nearly there.
Dropped my travel pass down beside the cab in Watford. The driver retrieved it at the terminus and checked I had it safely before leaving.
Another full bus drove straight past our Hertford stop at school pickup time. We need something bigger on that journey, not another apologetic wave.
Sitting over the rear axle towards Welwyn Garden City felt like joining a trampoline club. The rest of the journey was fine, but that suspension needs attention.
Since the timetable change, my Borehamwood feeder reaches the interchange just after the last onward bus leaves. Someone needs to compare the two timetables.
That working USB port on the Barnet bus saved my revision notes and probably my afternoon. Phone went from nearly dead to usable before college.
Front half of the New Barnet bus was warm; the back felt like a fridge. Moving seats helped, although balancing the temperature would help everyone.
Squinting at the dim destination display in Enfield drizzle is becoming a routine. Please replace whatever lights it, because waving at every bus gets old.
Clear stop announcements made my first trip through Wood Green straightforward. They could turn them down a touch upstairs, but I knew exactly where to get off.
Twenty peaceful minutes through Finchley with no rattling windows, sudden stops or unnecessary fuss. Honestly, that is all I want after work.
Sunday shopping in Potters Bar works if you plan your entire afternoon around the bus. A shorter gap around lunchtime would make it considerably more useful.
Platform 2 at Stevenage, 07:40, and the late train gained another ten minutes without explanation. My manager gets updates from me; passengers should get them too.
Found a suspicious brown smear across my seat leaving Hatfield. I stood instead, which rather defeated paying for a comfortable journey.
Logging into the Wi-Fi repeatedly between Welwyn Garden City and London got tedious. When it stayed connected, emails loaded perfectly well.
Useful warning at Hitchin that our train had fewer carriages today. Knowing where to stand saved everyone the usual last-second platform shuffle.
Lost tourist here. A member of staff at Finsbury Park pointed out the right platform and explained how to recognise my train without making me feel daft.
Six trips into King's Cross this fortnight, six arrivals when promised. Being able to stop adding a spare half-hour to everything feels quite luxurious.
Before I'd put the buggy brake on in Hatfield, we were moving. Drivers need to check the pushchair area rather than assume boarding means ready.
Extra capacity after school in Stevenage has made a noticeable difference. My son now gets home on the first bus, although Fridays still look tight.
Student prices are decent in St Albans, provided you carry the physical college card. Accepting the college's digital version would save a lot of awkward conversations.
Somehow my PE kit reached the Watford depot before I noticed it was missing. Lost property matched the description and had it ready after school.
Half-day finishes apparently don't exist to whoever schedules the Hertford school buses. Hundreds of pupils out at lunchtime, with the usual tiny service waiting for them.
Watching the driver explain the stop button to my nervous five-year-old made our Barnet trip easier. Friendly without holding the whole queue up.
Rain came through the roof above my school bag in Borehamwood. Wet exercise books are not a reasonable extra included with the fare.
Finally, a family ticket explained in plain English. The driver in Welwyn Garden City checked our group and sold us the cheapest suitable option.
Getting to the school entrance in Enfield involved a new diversion that wasn't on the printed route map. We arrived, but an updated map would prevent confusion.
Upstairs heating was completely dead on the 08:10 through Finchley. Everyone kept their coats zipped and one child was doing homework in gloves.
After a child was sick near Wood Green, the driver closed off the seats and arranged cleaning at the terminus. Sensible handling of an unpleasant situation.
Thank you for noticing my daughter had boarded while I was still folding the buggy. Keeping the doors open until we were together prevented a proper panic.
Buggy parking on the Potters Bar bus is fine once you're inside. Reaching it past the narrow middle-door partition takes more manoeuvring than it should.
Our school had arranged boarding help at Stevenage, yet nobody appeared where we'd been told to wait. Thirty children and two teachers should not be left guessing.
A toilet without soap or running water is particularly unhelpful when travelling with a toddler. Please check both before sending the train out from King's Cross.
Travelling from Hatfield with a small school group meant scattering the children across several sections. Advance advice on suitable departures would make supervising them easier.
Homework actually got done between Hitchin and Finsbury Park because the fold-down table stayed level. A little more elbow room would earn the fifth star.
Pushing twins through New Barnet was manageable with the lifts working. Better signs at the entrance would have saved us walking towards the stairs first.
When my child became frightened by the departure whistle, the platform worker explained it quietly and gave us time. Small kindness, much calmer journey home.
Ramp jammed at the kerb in Hertford and the driver had no alternative to offer. Being told to wait for another bus isn't an accessibility plan.
Lowering the bus properly in Watford made boarding with my walking stick straightforward. I wish the stop itself had a bit more room to turn.
Priority-seat stickers on the St Albans vehicle have faded almost completely. Nobody was unpleasant, but clearer markings would spare passengers having to explain themselves.
As a deaf passenger, I appreciated the Stevenage driver reading my phone and typing a reply. They spoke to me directly instead of turning to my friend.
Onboard screen stayed stuck on Hatfield long after we'd left. I rely on the visual stops, so a frozen display is more than a minor annoyance.
Reaching the wheelchair stop button in Barnet required twisting behind my shoulder. The space itself was adequate; moving that button would make it much better.
Apparently folding my walking frame was too much trouble for the driver to explain. A sharp gesture towards the aisle left me standing there feeling foolish.
Since audible stop names returned on my Borehamwood journey, I can travel independently again. Please keep checking that the system works before departure.
Boarded safely in Enfield, although the ramp was steep because the bus stopped well away from the kerb. Better positioning would make a real difference.
Pressing the bell produced neither a light nor a sound on the Wood Green bus. With limited vision, I had no way to know it had registered.
Bright edging around the front step in Finchley helped me judge it properly after dark. The contrasting handrail was useful too, though one grip felt loose.
Rather than moving my chair without asking, the Potters Bar driver explained the backrest position and waited for me to adjust. Exactly how assistance should work.
Reading the Welwyn Garden City timetable required my strongest glasses and a magnifier. All the information is there; printing it larger would make it usable.
Booked a ramp for Hatfield and watched my intended train leave without one arriving. The booking clearly existed because staff found it afterwards.
Accessible toilet was locked with cleaning supplies stored inside on the service from Stevenage. Essential passenger facilities should never become spare cupboards.
Wheelchair space towards King's Cross was generous, but the table edge pressed against my knees. A little adjustability would improve an otherwise usable area.
Using the hearing loop at the Finsbury Park assistance point made the conversation clear. Finding the small loop symbol took longer than the actual enquiry.
Unfamiliar with Potters Bar, I asked for the route avoiding steps. Staff walked to the junction with me and pointed out the lift rather than vaguely waving.
My sight-assistance request was passed between the teams at Hitchin and King's Cross correctly. Nobody made me start the explanation again at the other end.
First bus from Stevenage cancelled at 05:25, after I'd already reached the stop. Missing the start of a care shift isn't something I can shrug off.
Early-morning lighting on the Hatfield bus was pleasantly gentle without making the steps dark. Much appreciated by someone finishing a night shift.
Changing buses in Watford now involves 28 minutes beside a closed shopping centre. Both services run, but their evening times could fit together better.
Paying the same sensible fare after a late restaurant shift in St Albans deserves credit. Getting home shouldn't become a luxury once the shops close.
Last Hertford journey finished short of the destination printed at the stop. If the late service has a different terminus, say so before people board.
Driver change in Welwyn Garden City added twelve minutes to an otherwise smooth trip. Could the handover happen within the scheduled waiting time?
Phantom buses apparently work Saturdays in Borehamwood. The app counted ours down to due, then removed it while we were still standing there.
During the evening diversion in Barnet, the driver used the signed temporary stop under the lights and explained the walking route. That felt properly thought through.
Homeward from New Barnet after ten hours on my feet, the ventilation fan whined continuously. Journey time was good; the noise made resting impossible.
Breakfast passengers in Enfield shouldn't inherit last night's chips under every other seat. The first departure needs a proper sweep before it leaves the depot.
Illuminated STOP REQUESTED sign was easy to see on the late Wood Green service. Saved me wondering whether I'd pressed the bell firmly enough.
Someone has finally matched the Finchley hospital bus to the evening shift finish. Walking out and catching it without sprinting has changed my week.
Weekend workers exist in Potters Bar too. Sunday's first bus arrives too late for my shop opening, although the service is perfectly useful afterwards.
Replacement bus left Hatfield while passengers from the arriving train were still crossing the footbridge. Coordinating the transfer is surely part of arranging a replacement.
Post-gig train from Finsbury Park had nowhere near enough room for the queue. A predictable concert finish should prompt more capacity on the final departures.
Saturday engineering changes were posted where weekday commuters might notice them. Occasional travellers at Hertford North need a clearer warning near the ticket machines.
Catching the first train from Welwyn Garden City, I noticed even the window ledges had been wiped. One overflowing platform bin was the only let-down.
Despite the late hour, someone at King's Cross stayed available until our platform was confirmed. Much better than a row of shut windows and unanswered questions.
Adding a later northbound departure means I can finish a theatre shift and still reach Stevenage. I've already stopped budgeting for a taxi every Friday.
Wipers failed before we'd even left Watford properly, so the bus was withdrawn. Checking basic wet-weather equipment before departure might have saved a busload of missed appointments.
Nonslip flooring by the St Albans bus entrance coped well with everyone's dripping shoes. There was still a small puddle by the buggy space.
Fogged windows upstairs made the Hatfield journey feel like travelling inside a kettle. Some effective demisting would help passengers spot their stops.
Stepping onto a properly warmed bus in Stevenage during that frosty morning was bliss. Whoever started the heating before the first pickup deserves thanks.
Roof vents were jammed shut on a packed Hertford bus in humid weather. With no cooling working either, the whole journey felt stale and stuffy.
Cooling recovered quickly after each stop in Welwyn Garden City, even with the doors opening constantly. Slightly noisy, but worth it in that heat.
Forty minutes beside a broken-down bus in freezing Borehamwood, with no estimate for a replacement. The weather was bad; the lack of a rescue update was avoidable.
Flood diversion around Barnet came with a clear announcement naming the replacement stops. I could tell my mum where to meet me before we arrived.
Damp cushions on the New Barnet service suggested the windows had been left open in the rain. Most seats were dry, but nobody had marked the wet ones.
Condensation kept dripping from the Enfield bus ceiling onto my collar. A towel on the dashboard isn't going to sort the moisture collecting overhead.
Replacing the door seals has stopped the icy draught on my Wood Green commute. Still a little chilly near the rear exit, but much improved.
Gusty conditions through Finchley were handled with steady driving and extra space around parked vehicles. Arrived slightly later and entirely happy with that choice.
Paper timetable at the Potters Bar stop has turned to pulp inside its cracked case. The route is useful, assuming you already know when it runs.
Broken heater all the way from Hitchin, with frost still outside and no warmer carriage identified. My coat shouldn't have to do the train's job.
Hot air came out of the vents on an already sweltering train from King's Cross. Please test the cooling under actual summer conditions.
Wet-weather mats by the Stevenage train doors were saturated before we boarded. The rest of the carriage was tidy, but the entrance needed attention.
Gritted access to the Hatfield platform made an icy start manageable. A little patch near the shelter had been missed, which I reported.
Moving between carriages near Potters Bar didn't involve alternating between roasting and freezing. Sensible, consistent cooling, although the fan above my seat rattled slightly.
Following the storm, a replacement unit was ready when our damaged train was taken out of service. We changed trains at Stevenage with surprisingly little delay.
Destination blind promised Watford while the driver said this particular journey ended earlier. Correcting the display before picking people up would prevent a lot of arguments.
Visiting St Albans, I couldn't work out the ticket zones. The driver explained the boundary using two recognisable stops, which was far clearer than the leaflet.
Stop pole in Hertford used one name and the onboard screen used another. Both apparently meant the same place, but newcomers aren't born knowing that.
With a suitcase and no local knowledge, changing buses in Stevenage looked daunting. The driver identified the exact stand and the route number I needed.
Map for the Hatfield route contains a coloured line and almost no useful street names. Please add enough landmarks for someone unfamiliar with the area.
Side display showing the route number helped me identify the Welwyn Garden City bus from the queue. It would be even better without the scratched cover.
Nobody posted a notice at the closed Borehamwood stop. Three visitors waited there until a passer-by explained the diversion; the operator should have done that.
Simple pictures on the Barnet travel leaflet explained boarding, payment and stop requests without a wall of English. My visiting grandparents found it genuinely useful.
Picked up a New Barnet timetable with no publication date. It matched today's journey, but there's no way of knowing when the information becomes old.
Muffled speakers turned every Enfield announcement into a noise resembling someone talking through a scarf. Adjusting the volume won't fix a damaged speaker.
Fare list beside the Wood Green bus door let me choose before reaching the driver. Clear prices are especially welcome when you're visiting.
Asked whether my hotel was before or after the Finchley stop. The driver remembered and gave me a quiet reminder as we approached, which saved an unnecessary walk.
Relief driver through Potters Bar checked the route instructions several times while stopped. Sensible caution, though familiarisation beforehand would keep the service moving.
Screens still showed King's Cross after staff announced a different destination. Visitors shouldn't have to decide which of two official sources is telling the truth.
Platform alteration at Hitchin was announced barely two minutes before departure. That's not enough notice for people carrying luggage across the station.
Hertford North signs could do more to explain that the town's other station is separate. Staff clarified it, but the local map left us unsure.
Announcements on the train from Finsbury Park were slow enough for my visiting aunt to follow. Station names were clear, though the volume dipped near the doors.
Exit signs at New Barnet included the surrounding roads, so meeting our lift was straightforward. A map outside would have completed the picture.
Ticket-machine language settings defeated us at King's Cross. A patient employee walked through the choices with my dad and checked the tickets before we left.
Folded bike fitted the published conditions, yet the Watford driver refused it without checking. Clear rules are pointless if passengers get a different answer at the door.
Taking my elderly dog through St Albans was easy. The driver politely asked me to keep the aisle clear, and that was the whole conversation.
Luggage shelf on the Hatfield bus was too shallow for my modest weekend bag. A better retaining edge would make that space genuinely useful.
Returning from a trip with one arm in a sling, I couldn't lift my case aboard in Stevenage. The driver secured the bus and helped without any fuss.
Suitcases occupied several seats on the Hertford service while passengers stood. Some guidance from the driver would have freed room without upsetting anyone.
Little storage recess on the Welwyn Garden City vehicle kept my folded scooter out of everyone's way. Helpful layout, although the sign above it was difficult to read.
Doors closed on my shopping trolley as I got off in Borehamwood. Please check the exit is clear instead of rushing to beat the lights.
During our scheduled Barnet layover, staff offered water for my panting dog from the depot tap. An unexpectedly thoughtful bit of service on a hot afternoon.
Wearing a small backpack made the Finchley bus seat feel remarkably narrow. I put it on my lap, but the hard seat divider still dug in.
Loud sighs greeted my pushchair at New Barnet even though the bay was empty. Parents can follow the rules without being made to feel unwelcome.
Flat floor from the front door to the seats made carrying shopping home through Enfield much easier. A slightly wider turn past the cab would help further.
Two heavy bags, one forgotten umbrella, and a driver at Wood Green who checked the seats before I left. Saved me discovering the missing item in the next downpour.
Shared buggy and wheelchair space on the Potters Bar bus needs clearer instructions. Everyone wanted to cooperate, but nobody knew which seats should fold.
Cycle advice from the helpline contradicted what staff told me at Hitchin. I planned around the first answer and ended up unable to travel.
Dust on the luggage rack out of King's Cross left a grey stripe across my clean holdall. Cleaning above eye level appears to have been forgotten.
Bike space from Stevenage was welcome, but the wheel holder wouldn't comfortably fit my ordinary wider tyre. More versatile fittings would avoid awkward balancing.
Diagram showing where folded bikes should go made boarding at Hatfield quick. It answered the question before I had to block a doorway and ask.
Room beneath the table let my small dog settle on the journey from Welwyn Garden City. Legroom for me was tighter, but we managed happily.
Left my violin on the train into King's Cross and feared the worst. Staff contacted the arriving service team and reunited us before my lesson.
Charged twice for one trip through Watford and still waiting for a reply a week later. Fixing payment errors shouldn't require more effort than earning the money.
Transfer ticket worked across both St Albans buses without another charge. Good value, though the allowed transfer time could be printed more prominently.
Cash passengers in Hertford were asked for exact money because the driver had no change. Understandable occasionally, but starting with a proper float would help.
Refund for my cancelled Stevenage journey appeared without a chase through customer services. Getting that sorted automatically was a pleasant surprise.
Website quoted one fare to Hatfield and the reader charged a higher one. Update the prices everywhere when they change, please.
Tapping my phone on the Welwyn Garden City bus took a second instead of several attempts. The improved reader keeps the morning queue moving nicely.
Valid concessionary pass, eligible time, full fare demanded anyway in Borehamwood. Staff need proper training on the tickets their own operator accepts.
My son wasn't sure how to ask for a child ticket in Barnet. The driver quietly explained it and let him try again without embarrassing him.
Fare cap resets at midnight, which makes my overnight Enfield shift surprisingly expensive. A clearer explanation of the charging day would at least prevent surprises.
Purchased day ticket wouldn't scan on the Wood Green bus despite showing as active. The app and the reader really need to agree with each other.
Weekly pass now costs less than my usual separate Finchley journeys, even with one day working from home. A monthly comparison in the app would be handy.
Flat phone battery left me unable to open my Potters Bar ticket. Staff checked my purchase receipt and sorted the journey instead of immediately demanding another fare.
Return ticket to New Barnet was reasonable, but its evening expiry caught me out after dinner. Displaying that restriction beside the price would be fairer.
Machine at Hatfield took payment, froze, and printed nothing. With the assistance desk closed, I had no practical way to sort it before my train.
Asked an onboard ticket checker whether my student discount applied and got an impatient lecture. Explaining the options politely would have taken less time.
Off-peak restriction only became obvious near the end of the booking process for Stevenage. The price was good once I'd found an eligible departure.
Railcard option on the Hitchin ticket machine was easy to find and the saving appeared immediately. Could do with a quicker confirmation screen.
Season ticket stopped opening the gates at King's Cross, but the desk replaced it promptly. One form and a short wait was reasonable.
Delay claim needed a ticket photo and a few simple details, then the payment arrived as promised. Credit for making compensation straightforward after a bad journey.
Football crowd in Stevenage was entirely predictable, yet no extra buses appeared. Forty-five minutes in a queue after the match suggests nobody planned for the finish.
Queue marshals after the Watford concert kept people in order and explained which bus was next. The signs were small, but the staff made it work.
Plenty of bags got seats on the St Albans bus while I stood. A friendly reminder about keeping seats for passengers would probably have sorted it.
Argument brewing between shoppers and school pupils in Hertford was calmed with a fair explanation of the queue. Nobody got singled out or humiliated.
Rail replacement crowds swallowed the normal Hatfield bus queue and there was no sign separating them. Different boarding points need to be marked properly.
Staggered buses after the late cinema finish in Welwyn Garden City worked well. We didn't all have to cram onto the same departure.
Driver skipped our advertised estate loop near Borehamwood because the main road was busy. Saving time by leaving waiting passengers behind is not acceptable.
Market-day shuttle in Barnet let my dad manage his shopping without walking miles between stops. Short trips, sensible intervals and plenty of room for bags.
Both doors opened for boarding in Enfield, but nobody explained where to validate tickets. A sign or quick announcement would prevent the confused shuffling.
Already packed bus in Wood Green kept taking passengers until people were pressed against the doors. Please respect the vehicle's capacity instead of squeezing more aboard.
School crowd rushed upstairs in Finchley and the driver asked them to use the handrails before moving. Firm, sensible and completely free of shouting.
Packed Potters Bar bus still made room for my wheelchair because the driver organised the space calmly. I wasn't left negotiating with strangers on my own.
Usually roomy school service through New Barnet turned up as a smaller bus today. We fitted, just, but substitutions need to reflect how busy that run gets.
One carriage stayed locked while the rest of the train from Stevenage was crushed full. Nobody explained why or arranged enough usable capacity.
Event crowd arrived at Finsbury Park to find no staff directing people towards the quieter boarding areas. Better positioning of the station team would have helped.
Speakerphone conversations competed across the carriage from Hatfield. An occasional reminder to use headphones would improve the atmosphere without turning staff into classroom teachers.
Carriage loading display at King's Cross pointed me towards the less crowded end. It was broadly accurate and saved a lengthy stand.
After the match, station staff kept a clear route along the Stevenage platform edge. Boarding took a little longer but felt much more controlled.
Extra carriages were ready before the bank holiday rush at Hitchin. Our walking group boarded together without displacing everyone already waiting.
Loose seat shifted sideways every time we turned through Watford. I moved, told the driver and would expect that seat taken out of use immediately.
Persistent dashboard rattle on my usual St Albans bus has finally gone. Amazing how one repaired panel can make a whole commute less irritating.
Very clean Hertford bus, unfortunately smelling strongly enough of disinfectant to make my eyes water. Less product, properly diluted, would be an improvement.
Reported graffiti on a Stevenage seat yesterday and found it removed today. Quick maintenance makes the bus feel cared for.
Engine fumes drifted into the Hatfield saloon whenever we stopped. That needs checking at the depot, not masking with an open window.
Small bag hook beside my Welwyn Garden City seat kept shopping off the wet floor. Handy detail, though a second hook would have been welcome.
Emergency exit in Borehamwood had operator equipment stacked in front of it. Those boxes need a proper storage location before the vehicle carries passengers.
Under-seat chewing gum has actually been removed from the Barnet bus, rather than cleaned around. Anyone who's caught a trouser leg on it will understand my delight.
Advertising screen repeated the same noisy clip throughout the New Barnet journey. Useful service information would be welcome; that soundtrack definitely wasn't.
Seat cushion on the Enfield service had worn so thin I could feel the frame. Twenty minutes was enough to leave my back aching.
Front seat folded up neatly on the Wood Green bus, giving my rollator somewhere secure to stand. Release handle could be a brighter colour.
Glasses slipped into a dark gap beside my Finchley bus seat. At the terminus the driver found a torch and helped retrieve them without damaging the frame.
Window latch on the Potters Bar vehicle kept rattling loose, letting in traffic noise. A small repair would improve an otherwise comfortable bus.
Sewage smell spread well beyond the toilet on the train from King's Cross. Closing the toilet door did nothing; that unit needed attention before departure.
Socket beside my seat out of Stevenage wouldn't hold a plug properly. Charging only worked if I kept one hand against it, which rather limited its usefulness.
Rhythmic clunking beneath the carriage from Hitchin made concentrating difficult. We arrived on time, but the running noise deserves a maintenance check.
Refurbished seats on the Hatfield service have noticeably better cushioning. I'd still choose a little more back support for a longer ride.
Tinted windows reduced the glare enough to read my laptop approaching Finsbury Park. Reflections from the ceiling lights were the only remaining nuisance.
Onboard cleaner collected empty cups before the bins overflowed on our train from Welwyn Garden City. Keeping on top of it made a busy service feel civilised.
Saw the Watford driver handling a phone while we were moving. I've reported the journey details because that requires proper management action.
Complaint about my St Albans journey received a specific reply explaining the fault and repair date. Much more useful than a generic apology.
Not a word from the Hertford driver when I said good morning. Safe driving throughout, so no disaster, but a little acknowledgement would improve things.
Temporary works blocked my usual Stevenage stop, so the driver checked with control and explained the authorised alternative. Good to see a practical answer found promptly.
Helpline said my Hatfield ticket covered the diverted route; driver said it didn't. Staff need the same briefing before passengers become the messengers.
Personal apology for the delay into Welwyn Garden City sounded sincere and included the reason. We were still late, but at least treated like people.
Simple question about a Borehamwood stop got repeated back sarcastically to the queue. I don't expect a guided tour, just a civil answer.
Trainee driver in Barnet had a calm mentor who answered passenger questions while letting them concentrate. Training felt properly supported rather than improvised.
Email question about the New Barnet timetable eventually got a useful answer, five days later. Fine for next month, not so helpful for tomorrow.
Bell rang clearly before my Enfield stop, yet we sailed past it. The driver admitted forgetting, but I was still left walking back in the rain.
Damaged paper pass was replaced by post after one call to the Wood Green service team. Efficient process, though collection locally would have been quicker.
At the Finchley terminus, the driver noticed an older passenger seemed confused and called the supervisor to help. Nobody hurried them off onto the pavement.
Printed notices on the Potters Bar bus say to contact customer services but omit the opening hours. The number works; knowing when someone answers would improve it.
Cancellation only appeared at Stevenage after the train's departure time had passed, although staff said they'd known earlier. Timely notice could have saved my appointment.
Two employees at Hatfield directed replacement-bus passengers to opposite sides of the station. Agree a boarding point before sending a tired crowd back and forth.
Driver explained our signal delay near Welwyn Garden City using several technical abbreviations. I appreciated the update, but plain English would have made it useful.
After reporting a recurring fault on the Hitchin service, I received a follow-up confirming what had been repaired. Nice to know the report reached someone practical.
Asked about a complicated onward route at Finsbury Park. The employee checked the journey details carefully instead of guessing, although it took a few minutes.
Recovering from shoulder surgery, I struggled to lift my bag at King's Cross. A staff member noticed, asked permission and carried it to the assistance meeting point.
Three Watford buses arrived together after a 45-minute gap. Spreading them out would serve considerably more people than running a little convoy.
Same minutes past each hour in St Albans are easy to remember. That regular pattern makes spontaneous errands possible, even if evenings remain less frequent.
Route into Hertford loops around several estates before reaching the interchange. Necessary coverage, perhaps, but a quicker connecting option at peak times would be useful.
Summer timetable in Stevenage finally allows enough recovery time between trips. The bus now starts the return journey punctually instead of carrying yesterday's optimism around.
Ten minutes through lunchtime Hatfield traffic is a fantasy, yet that's what the timetable allows. Publish achievable journey times so passengers can plan honestly.
Restoring evening calls at our Welwyn Garden City estate stop has shortened my walk home. One later Friday trip would make the improvement even better.
Second cancellation this week in Borehamwood because no relief driver was available. Breaks are essential, which is why the staffing plan needs to cover them.
New departure after the Barnet industrial estate's early Friday finish is spot on. For once the timetable seems designed around when people actually leave work.
Shortened daytime route in New Barnet now means changing buses with all my shopping. Faster for through passengers, but harder for those making local trips.
Saturday Enfield route differs from the weekday version, with no clear distinction on the stop map. A separate line or label would prevent wasted journeys.
School-holiday dates are now printed beside the Wood Green departures they affect. Saves parents trying to decode a tiny letter at the bottom.
Revised Finchley interchange now gives me six minutes between buses instead of an impossible dash. Both drivers kept to the new times all week.
Intermediate stops around Potters Bar only show rough estimates, which vary quite a lot. Adding a couple of proper timing points would make boarding more predictable.
Hertford North stop was removed from our journey after boarding to recover lost time. Improving the arrival figure elsewhere doesn't help passengers carried beyond their destination.
Losing alternate midday trains from Enfield Chase leaves an awkward hole for appointments. The remaining service needs strengthening before the timetable is cut like that.
Fast and stopping departures at King's Cross looked similar until their calling points appeared. Showing the stopping pattern sooner would make choosing less stressful.
Even spacing of departures from Potters Bar suits my unpredictable finishing time. Missing one no longer turns into a disproportionate wait.
Connection at Finsbury Park allowed enough time to use the stairs without running. Another couple of minutes would help with luggage, but this was workable.
During planned works, staff explained the alternative route and confirmed my existing ticket covered it. Reaching Hitchin without buying anything extra took the sting out of the diversion.
USB socket on the Watford bus became hot and smelled burnt when connected. I unplugged immediately and reported it; electrical fittings need proper checks.
Guest Wi-Fi on the St Albans service connected without demanding my birthday and life story. Fair speed for browsing, with a brief drop near the terminus.
Charging is available on the Hertford bus, but only through older USB ports. Adding USB-C would help passengers whose newer cables don't fit.
Live route map on the Stevenage bus showed our actual progress, including the diversion. Easily the most useful screen I've seen on public transport.
Pale grey departure text in the Hatfield bus app is almost unreadable with my eyesight. A high-contrast setting should be part of a basic travel app.
Stop display in Welwyn Garden City now agrees with the app after weeks of different predictions. Still shifts by a minute or two, but far more trustworthy.
Fault-report form for the Borehamwood service wouldn't work with my screen reader. An inaccessible complaints system makes reporting inaccessible buses particularly frustrating.
Working induction loop by the Barnet driver's cab let me hear the fare explanation clearly. Usually the engine noise overwhelms that conversation.
Socket location on the New Barnet bus meant my charging cable crossed the space where feet go. Useful feature, awkward positioning.
FREE WI-FI stickers everywhere on the Enfield vehicle, but no network appeared on anyone's phone. Please switch it on or take the promise down.
Downloading the Wood Green timetable for offline use worked well when my signal disappeared. A clearer download button would make that feature easier to discover.
Automatic screen dimming on the Finchley bus keeps stop names readable at night without lighting up the whole upstairs. Someone has thought about actual passengers.
QR feedback survey on the Potters Bar bus demanded a fleet number I couldn't find inside. Put the identifying number beside the code and I'll gladly report faults.
Help point at New Barnet rang unanswered for several minutes after the ticket office closed. A button labelled assistance needs someone available at the other end.
Departure screen at King's Cross switched to advertising while we were waiting for disruption details. Service information should stay visible when journeys are going wrong.
Only alternate seats had power sockets on my train from Hatfield. Sharing worked after some negotiation, but more even provision would be better.
Wi-Fi sign-in page on the Stevenage service now works properly when I enlarge the text. Took one attempt, although the final connect button remains rather small.
Board at Hitchin highlighted the two omitted stops in a changed service instead of making us compare long lists. Very helpful, once the message appeared.
When the Finsbury Park screens failed, staff put up handwritten platform updates and refreshed them regularly. Basic materials, excellent communication.
Pulling away in Watford while the rear door was still open was frightening. Whatever failed, the vehicle needs checking before carrying another load of passengers.
Approaching speed humps gently through St Albans made a huge difference to my sore back. We lost barely any time and nobody bounced out of their seat.
Grab handles on the Hertford bus are too high for several of us shorter school pupils. Lower straps would make standing less of a balancing exercise.
Cycling alongside the Stevenage route, I noticed the driver wait for a safe passing gap instead of squeezing through. That's the kind of driving that builds trust.
